new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word; the only stated exception is a small set of trisyllabic fully-reduplicated words (CVCV-CVC type, e.g. paŋapaŋ), which take primary stress on the first (antepenultimate) syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned only for the reduplicated trisyllabic exception class: secondary stress on the ultima (third syllable), e.g. paŋapaŋ 'moon', suhusuh 'Triton trumpet shell'. Nothing said about secondary stress in ordinary longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Small group of trisyllabic reduplicated words: primary stress on antepenult, secondary on ultima. Blust (1996:26) additionally notes that in genitive compounds primary stress was recorded on the first vowel of the head, giving apparent surface contrasts ([pulixixi] 'corn, callus' vs [kanisus] 'milk'), while affirming stress is not phonemic. Note also (1.1, p. 6) vowels of monosyllables are lengthened in isolation/sentence-final position; word-final consonants are analysed as extraprosodic (1.2), which is consistent with penult stress counting open syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('penultimate syllable of a word'); based on 13 months of fieldwork (2003-2004) across six Ninigo communities. The companion Organised Phonology Data paper (Wilson & Wozna 2005:53) gives the same rule in nearly identical words and adds 'There is no contrastive tone in Seimat.' No instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe Seimat of the Ninigo Islands (seim1238, ISO ssg) as a whole; Wozna & Wilson's data come from Pihon, Liot, Amix, Lau, Mal and Patexux communities, Blust 1996 from a single speaker. No dialect split is asserted for the stress rule. (Blust 1996 also gives a separate penult-stress description for Wuvulu-Aua, wuvu1239, pp. ~15-16 of the same file — not Seimat.)

sources.note: 'Suprasegmentals', p. 53: no contrastive length, tone or stress; 'Stress normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word except in a small group of 3 syllable words where reduplication occurs. In this case the primary stress occurs on the first syllable and secondary stress on the third syllable, e.g. <pangapang> moon, <suhusuh> Triton trumpet shell.'

sources.note: p. 26: 'Stress in Seimat generally falls on the penultimate syllable, although in genitive compounds primary stress was recorded on the first vowel of the head, resulting in some apparent stress contrasts... Although the stress rules of Seimat remain to be worked out in detail, it is clear that stress is not phonemic.' (single-speaker data).
